1:
The name is a puzzle and all of them work at it. Calvin lays the options out: the hearth of the great altar, the city being the seat of a fire that will issue from it to consume God's enemies; or the fire couching on that altar like a lion; or, on the common derivation, the lion of God, denoting the strength by which the place overcame its enemies. Henry prefers the lion: king among beasts as Jerusalem was among cities, head-city of a tribe whose ensign was a lion; while she was righteous she was bold as one. He allows the altar reading and sets it aside, taking the doubled name for a woe upon Jerusalem, repeated as one who wept over her repeated it, to be the more awakening.

Ellicott asks what kind of word it is. He groups it with other poetic surnames for cities and nations, and suggests the prophet coined it, or that it belonged to the secret language of the prophetic schools, as one cipher stood for Babel, another for Egypt, and in later hands Edom for Rome. Then he glances at his own century, where speech has the same trick of names of praise and scorn for England and France, John Bull and the British Lion, Crapaud and the Gallic Cock, and remarks that these scarcely rise to the level of poetry. He allows both lion and hearth, preferring the lion because the same word names men of exceptional heroism elsewhere, and notes that the prophet interprets his own riddle in the next phrase, the city where David encamped.

The instruction to add year to year is heard as sarcasm, Ellicott taking the word to imply the solemn keeping of the new year festival. Wesley makes it plain: go on killing sacrifices year after year, thinking to appease him, and all of it will be in vain. Clarke sets the chapter in a series: the subject here and in the four following is Sennacherib's invasion, the distress while it lasted, the sudden deliverance, the prosperity after, interspersed with reproofs for hypocrisy and for leaning on Egypt; and the whole, he warns, is not one continued discourse but a collection of discourses on one subject.

Then the woe itself, and the name turns round on the city. Ellicott renders it that she shall be to him as Ariel, so the name does not falsify itself: in the middle of her heaviness she is still the lion of God, or his altar-hearth. Calvin makes the reversal grim, an altar being where victims of every kind are slaughtered and the whole city to overflow with blood; outward profession and ceremony and even the visible tokens of favour, he concludes, are worth nothing without sincere obedience. Clarke offers two futures, the place all on flame as when the Chaldeans took it or covered with carcasses as when the Romans did, the more distant perhaps glanced at in an obscure phrase without being its subject.

The siege is described in a word nobody translates alike. Clarke reports that some read like David where the text has another word, a reading the Greek and several manuscripts support and a bishop adopted, and rejects it as harsh and unnecessary; he does accept a correction of forts to towers on like evidence. Calvin hears in the word the roundness of a ball and takes it for encirclement, every way of escape cut off. Delitzsch marks where the woe stops unfolding and the words of promise begin. Ellicott furnishes the scene from the Assyrian sculptures, the mound thrown up against the wall, the battering-ram set on it. Gill and Calvin agree on what matters most: the besieger named here is God, the Assyrians undertaking nothing but at his command however their passions hurry them, and the prophecy is the more terrible for it.
4:
The voice from the dust is explained from the trade of the necromancers. Clarke sets out the belief, popular among heathens as well as Jews and traceable in Homer and Horace, that the dead uttered a feeble grating sound unlike the human voice; and explains how it was produced, the practitioners, chiefly women, having an art of speaking with a feigned voice formed not by the organs of speech but deep in the chest or belly, whence the Greek name surviving in our ventriloquist. They could make the voice seem to come from underground or from a distance, the better to impose on those who consulted them. Ellicott keeps panic: the besieged whisper like the spectres heard in a soothsayer's inner chamber, the war-cry of the brave become the tone of those that peep and mutter.

Calvin reads the verse as a study in what humiliation does not do. He supplies the implied contrast: the men addressed had carried their heads high and despised everyone, venturing to curse God and mock at his word, and now that pride is laid low. But he refuses the comfortable inference: they do not change their dispositions, shame merely restraining the wantonness they formerly indulged, so the haughty voice comes out low and confused as from a cavern.

Whose the strangers are decides who is being threatened. Calvin states the majority view first, that foreigners means enemies and the multitude oppressing the Jews will be innumerable as dust; then, examining the passage, he adopts the contrary opinion, that the prophet speaks contemptuously of the garrisons the Jews relied on, strong men taken into pay from a distance, so they dreaded no danger. Wesley reaches the same in a line, the strangers being those they hired and the terrible ones their own commanders and stout soldiers. Ellicott keeps the enemies, brought low by a sudden catastrophe under the threshing instrument of God's judgments.

Then a visitation, and the pronoun matters. Gill insists it is not the strangers who are visited but Ariel herself, punished for her own sins with the Romans as instrument, and fills the storm with portents: a great voice in the temple saying let us depart hence, comets, chariots and armed men in the air, a gate opening of itself. Ellicott is not sure the language is metaphor at all, and allows that some terrific storm, acting as an angel of the Lord, burst at once on the city and the host encamped against her, bringing safety to one and destruction to the other. Calvin uses the storm as contrast: what is chaff to a devouring flame, or dust to a whirlwind, and what can a garrison do when God has determined to chastise.

The closing figure divides them, and Calvin explains why. Others, he says, take it for consolation, the enemies of the church being dreamers whose hopes God disappoints just as they think the prize won; he grants great plausibility, calls the doctrine excellent, and rejects it as not agreeing with the text. Then he says why such readings prevail: when a sentence is beautiful it attracts us, and causes us to steal away from the true meaning, so that we do not adhere closely to the context or spend much time investigating what the author meant. His own reading makes the Jews the dreamers, hungry men asleep who had refused the feasts of the word and imagined abundance, and will find on waking how insubstantial it was. Clarke takes the enemies instead and insists the point is not their vanishing but their disappointment; he calls the comparison elegant in the highest degree, natural but not obvious, appealing to inward feelings rather than outward senses, and fit to stand beside a famous passage of Virgil improved from Homer. Delitzsch calls the whole an enigma of the future which the prophet holds out before his contemporaries' eyes.
9:
Four readings of the opening verb, disagreeing even on its mood. Ellicott makes it astonish yourselves, the form implying the astonishment was self-caused; he pictures the prophet reciting what he has just delivered to disciples and people, who are staggered and incredulous, and breaking into vehement reproof; the shift from second person to third means he paused to describe their condition as an observer might. Calvin reports the rendering be amazed and prefers another: let them dwell on the thought as long as they please, it ends only in a mind amazed, God's judgment so overwhelming them that they may torture themselves with thinking and still find no outlet. Gill takes it as an instruction to stop and consider, the Jewish commentators placing the address in Ahaz's reign or directing it to the men of Zion. Clarke renders an imperative to dither: go on what-what-whatting in a state of mental indetermination till the overflowing scourge takes them away.

Who is spoken to divides them almost as much. Gill notes the general opinion that the words go to the sober part, then observes that the next verse shows the case was general and those addressed as stupid as the rest. Henry keeps the sober remnant and gives them a task, to be affected with their neighbours' carelessness; he offers an alternative in which the others delay and put off repentance and sport themselves with their own deceivings, while these cry out, lament the folly, and pray for them.

The drunkenness is of another kind. Ellicott points out that these are men outwardly too drunk to understand, but not on wine or the palm-juice which, an earlier chapter said, they habitually did indulge in; this drunkenness is of another type. Calvin makes it spiritual: it engrosses and stupefies all the senses till men are blind to the plainest subjects, and when God shows the brightest light of justice they are so dazzled that their dim sight bewilders them further.

Then the cause is named, and it is God. Gill takes it as a giving up to a reprobate mind, fulfilled in those who chose darkness rather than light, and notes the apostle produces the passage in proof. Calvin puts the logic carefully: as it belongs to God to give eyes and enlighten, so he alone takes the light away, and does it when he sees that by a depraved hatred of the truth we of our own accord wish for darkness. Ellicott calls it judicial blindness and finds keen irony in the word for rulers standing in apposition with the seers, emphasised because they did not see; they are like men who have wrapped the mantle round the head to sleep. Delitzsch makes the stupefaction self-inflicted, punishment of the dead works by which they mocked God and deceived themselves.

The sealed book is the figure for the result. Calvin insists the stupidity runs through every rank, learned and unlearned alike dazzled and seeing no more in the word than in a sealed letter; he links it to the earlier precept upon precept, since men who never leave the first rudiments never reach solid doctrine, and is careful to say the doctrine is not taken away, only that having it they lack reason to use it. Ellicott takes the whole vision for the prophet's teaching, perhaps already written down, and divides the two refusals: the wise of this world treat the dark sayings as seals forbidding study, while the poorer unlearned plead a more genuine and less guilty ignorance, though the effect is the same. Gill puts the sealing in the readers, not the writing: sealed unto you and not unto others. Wesley explains that books were then sometimes rolls, so one is delivered unsealed and opened. Clarke restores a word the copies lost, so the answer reads I cannot read it.
13:
The charge is a split between mouth and heart. Calvin uses it to show the severity already announced rests on righteous grounds: men contend with God as if he were unjustly harsh, but the blame lies wholly with those who provoked him, and drawing near with the lips while the heart is far off is his definition of hypocrisy. He defends his rendering against those who translate the verb to be compelled or to magnify oneself, the contrasting word later deciding it. Wesley states both halves plainly: they draw near in worship and outward devotion, but do not pay the love and fear and obedience required.

The second half of the charge is about where the worship came from. Ellicott finds an anticipated Pharisaism: beside the great commandments and the prophets' incisive teaching there was already growing a traditional system of ethics built on wrong principles, ending in dishonest casuistry and formal devotion, its commentaries darkening counsel by words without knowledge as they would again in the Mishna and Gemara. Clarke works on the text, reading with the Greek and Chaldee that their fear is vain while they teach the commandments of men, and noting the divine name many manuscripts supply.

The punishment is aimed high. Calvin points out that the blinding falls not on the ordinary ranks but on the wise men the people admired, the leaders who ought to have been the body's eyes; the common people are blind already, like the other members, and if the eyes go dark what becomes of the rest? He asks what punishment is more dreadful than stupidity of mind, which men rarely perceive the greatness of, though it is the worst of all. Ellicott states the doom as a rule: not loving the light, they lose what they had and are left to a self-chosen blindness. History was to repeat itself, he adds, the words fulfilled in an age and manner beyond the prophet's horizon. Delitzsch makes it an instance of the universal law by which God meets the froward with frowardness.

Then a woe on men who plan underground. Calvin calls them diggers, who dig themselves lurking-places hoping to deceive God, and traces their confidence to settled contempt: they think there is no other way of being wise than to be skilful at mocking, count religion foolish simplicity, and hide in their cunning as in a labyrinth. The disease was already at work in the prophet's day, he observes, hypocrites mocking inwardly at God and despising prophecies. Wesley takes the metaphor from men digging to bury something, imagining they can deceive not men only but God by their professions. Ellicott offers two candidates for the secret: dark sensualities under the surface of the religion, or, as he thinks likelier, clandestine negotiations with Egypt or Babylon against the Assyrian instead of trusting the Lord of hosts. Delitzsch supplies the precedent, a king who kept his own appeal to Assyria quiet.

The last verse is hard to construe, and everyone says so. Calvin sets out the difficulty, which turns on two particles and a noun that may mean turning, the purposes formed in the heart, or turning upside down and so destruction; the received sense makes God say he would care no more about destroying them than a potter about turning his clay. He inclines away from it because the two particles look contrasted. Ellicott takes the opening as an exclamation, O your perversity, and calls the received English scarcely intelligible; as a question it becomes shall the potter be counted as the clay, which is the perversity meant, men inverting the relation of Creator and creature and behaving as atheists who deny any divine order they belong to. Gill allows both the perverseness and the revolving of schemes that inverts things. Wesley keeps the clay and the potter who disposes it as he sees fit.
17:
The answer to men who turn things upside down is that God will do it his own way. Henry puts the retort so and adds the challenge, let us see whose word shall stand; those who disbelieve providence are told to wait a little and be convinced by ocular demonstration that a God governs the world and orders its changes for his church's good. He allows the promise a first reference to the settlement after the Assyrian was beaten off, and then lets it look further. Ellicott hears not arbitrary sovereignty but a love that fulfils itself.

Which mountain stands for whom divides them, and Calvin will not decide it on elegance. Many, he reports, make the Jews the fruitful field because they are to become barren, and Christians the forest because they will yield abundance; the opinion is certainly plausible, he says, since men are usually gratified by anything ingenious, but a parallel passage later settles the prophet's own use of the figure against it. Clarke takes the ingenious reading and presses it, finding the principal view beyond the revolutions then at hand in the rejection of the Jews and calling of the Gentiles; the first had been God's vineyard, watered in vain and now to be given up for a wilderness, the last barren till grace made them fruitful.

Then a promise that Calvin thinks needs defending. Isaiah appears to contradict himself, he says, having foretold a stupidity among God's people so great that nobody would understand, and now saying the deaf shall understand and the blind see. His answer is a sequence: the Church must first be chastised and purified, and the promise belongs to what comes out of that judgment. Ellicott sets the open vision against the self-chosen ignorance of the sealed book, and takes the volume named here for the prophet's own message or the law understood at last in its fulness, so the doom of closed eyes pronounced at his call holds no longer.

The joy is contested in a smaller way. Calvin rejects the rendering that has them add to or continue their rejoicing, since what is described is not a joy prolonged but a new one, given to people at present distressed; and he draws the rule that afflictions prepare us to receive grace, God casting us down to raise us up, so his people should not lose heart under correction but expect better things. Ellicott makes the joy a new element, since men had grown weary of the very name of the Holy One of Israel, and in the better time that name becomes the source of joy for the poor and lowly the prophet watched with most sympathy. Wesley makes them the mean and despicable, such as most of the first Christians were.

Last the enemies, and the question is which. Ellicott keeps them contemporary, the terrible one the Assyrian invader and the scorner those who derided the prophet's message and watched for a fault to make an accusation. Gill refuses the Assyrian and works forward, through the rulers who persecuted the first Christians, the Roman power broken under Constantine, and the Roman antichrist still to be brought down. Calvin is interested in the classes rather than the names, distinguishing those who are openly wicked and have no shame from those who keep an appearance of goodness and are no better; and he explains why their removal matters: while the bad are mixed with the good and even hold the highest place, everything is soiled, God is neither worshipped nor feared, and godliness is trampled. Only when they are subdued is the Church restored to its splendour and the godly, freed from their distresses, leap for joy. Delitzsch adds that the incorrigible would be given up to destruction, so the people coming out of that judgment would have nothing of the kind to expect again.
21:
Making a man an offender for a word admits two constructions. Gill takes it of a word inadvertently spoken or wilfully misconstrued, or of preaching the word at all, the character of persecutors in every age; he reports the other rendering, that they make a man sin by a word, which a Jewish commentator applies to the false prophets. Ellicott prefers the first: the prophet had been accused, as a later one would be, of want of patriotism for rebuking Israel and its rulers; the alternative has them suborning false witnesses. Calvin describes the mechanism from the other side: men wanting unbounded licence bore reproof impatiently and watched the prophets' words to catch them out or fasten a false construction on them, which is where calumnies and ensnaring questions come from, spread like nets.

The gate is a courtroom, and Clarke furnishes it from travel. He quotes a traveller reporting that in Algiers the treasurer, the master of the horse and the other officers of the regency sit constantly in the palace gate for the distribution of justice; the Ottoman court, he adds, seems to have been called the Porte for the same reason, from the justice and business transacted in its gateways. He renders the phrase accordingly as pleading in the gate. Ellicott keeps the preaching, in the open air at the places of public concourse, before the rulers as they sat. Wesley notes that the people assembled there on civil and sacred business, and prophets prophesied there.

The last charge is emptiness. Ellicott points out that the Hebrew word is the one used of the formlessness before creation, so the accusations brought against the prophet were incoherent and absolutely chaotic in their falsehood. Then the answer opens with a title, which Ellicott makes vivid from a Jewish tradition that Abraham had been accused before Nimrod by his kinsmen for refusing to worship the host of heaven; that history assured the prophet God would not abandon him to his accusers either. Clarke takes a preposition as a noun, giving the God of the house of Jacob, and reports a scholar's doubt about the verb for waxing pale, read here alone and carrying no sense of shame in the cognate languages.

Jacob is imagined watching. Ellicott has the patriarch appear as another does elsewhere, watching his descendants' fortunes with changing emotions, shame and terror till now, the dawn of a better day at last. Calvin fixes the moment it is for: the people enslaved, the temple overturned, the sacrifices gone, when it might be thought religion had fallen and no deliverance was possible; the prediction was the plank left to shipwrecked men, to be seized and brought by into harbour.

Who sees whom in the next verse is uncertain. Clarke reads a different form with the Greek and Syriac, so the children see the work of God's hands rather than being seen. Ellicott suspects the work of mine hands is the verb's direct object and his children an interpretative insertion to explain a change from singular to plural. Calvin keeps the received sense and finds the redemption in the word children, those God adopts being made new men, citing the psalm about a people yet to be created praising the Lord. Gill has the church watching Jacob's posterity born again and nursed at her side; Wesley reverses the direction and has the believing seed of Jacob look at Gentiles whom they had begotten by the gospel, incorporated with them into one body. Delitzsch gives only the two verses, without comment. On the closing promise Calvin notes that some translate the murmurers whisperers and others wanderers, prefers those who could not endure the prophets' warnings, and remarks that God brings back men highly unworthy of it; Ellicott would read instruction for doctrine, the word belonging to the wisdom books, and notes how rare the verb for murmuring is.
